claims.claim: Tock timekeeping records — the underlying support for 'actual time and material costs' billed to federal partners under signed IAAs — cannot show who actually authored a given entry: when the Tock team enters hours on behalf of an absent employee, 'the timesheet has no field for who submitted the entry, so an entry made by the Tock team and an entry made by the employee are the same record afterwards,' and the timekeeping manager's weekly check only confirms a timecard exists, not who filed it. Because 18F represents these hours to client agencies as the employee's actual billable time (per the IAA billing and monthly-accounting terms), a record whose authorship cannot be reconstructed creates exposure if a client or auditor later challenges the accuracy of a specific charge.

State/local IGCA request letters may be signed by a delegated official instead of the chief executive, but the underlying delegation or authorizing statute is only orally 'confirmed' by the account manager — 'the instrument itself is not collected, and it is not one of the items assembled into the package that goes for review and signature.' Every other IAA/IGCA component (SOW, cost estimate, advance payment waiver) is expressly routed through the Agreements Team and OGC review before execution, but the one document that would prove the signer had authority to bind the state or city is never captured in the record OGC reviews, leaving the agreement's enforceability against the non-federal partner resting on an unverified, undocumented assertion.

Once a Slack account is converted to Single-Channel Guest during offboarding, its 2FA is disabled and its email is changed to a personal address the organization does not administer — meaning the account-recovery path ('forgot my password') for that identity now runs through a mailbox nobody at TTS controls. Because Slack messages are federal records 'attributable back to you' that must be managed as such, any post-conversion activity traceable to that account can no longer be reliably attributed to the departed individual rather than to whoever controls the personal mailbox, undermining the chain of custody records-management policy assumes.

The Office of Solutions describes each of its initiatives (cloud.gov, Login.gov, USWDS, etc.) as a 'standing commitment' with 'none of them carr[ying] an end date,' yet the same page states they are funded 'the same way engagement work is: out of reimbursements recovered against agreements that each name a period of performance.' TTS's agreements mechanism caps funding to what cumulative 7600Bs obligate and to the period of performance stated on the 7600A/7600B, and work cannot legally continue once an agreement lapses. A commitment represented to agencies and the public as perpetual is therefore structurally dependent on a funding instrument that is, by its own terms, finite — creating a recurring gap-in-authority risk every time an underlying agreement expires before renewal.

RFC-004's cross-TTS hiring pilot caps the pool of candidates a hiring manager may select for interview and folds mid-cycle replacement requests into that same capped, ranked pool ('drawn from the same capped pool, in the order the manager selects'), while TTS's Hiring Manager Guide obligates hiring managers to ensure Merit Systems Principles are followed throughout the process. Whether a discretionary, capacity-driven cap on who gets considered — applied identically to new hires and to replacements for existing engagement staff — remains consistent with merit-based, fair-and-open competition requirements is a Merit Systems Principles compliance question that should be routed to GSA/OHRM legal counsel for review before or during the pilot, not resolved by TTS program staff.
